title: Local businesses that also sell online
metaTitle: A local shop with two clear paths
excerpt: A local business that also sells online has two jobs: the visit and the shipment. Give each a path from the first screen so the address and the product do not share one button.
alt: Three hands holding coffee cups together over a wooden table, two with latte art, a visit in the room beside the separate question of what the shop ships.
caption: Cups on a wooden table. The visit and the shipment are different jobs. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the homepage of a local shop that also ships include?
faqs.answer: Two verbs, such as visit and shop, with the one that matches the real business as the primary action. Say the city and whether you ship in the same breath. A single button labeled explore makes both kinds of customer guess.

faqs.question: What belongs on the visit page?
faqs.answer: Hours in text, the address a person can copy, and what they can do in the room that they cannot do online. Add parking or a buzzer only if it changes whether they can get in. A booking path, if you have one, is part of the visit.

faqs.question: How should the online shop handle shipping cost?
faqs.answer: Show the shipping cost, or the rule that sets it, before the last step of checkout. Baymard's average of documented cart-abandonment studies is 70.22 percent, and extra costs are a reason shoppers name. Let people check out as a guest when you can.

markdown:
A local business that also sells online is doing two jobs. One job is the visit: hours, place, what to expect when someone walks in. The other job is the shipment: the product, the price, the delivery, the return. A local business website and shop gives each job its own path from the first screen.

The address and the product can share a brand. They should not fight for the same button. A visitor with a spare hour and a visitor in another city are both legitimate. They are not the same click.

## Two paths from the first screen

Name both jobs in the hero, in words. "Visit the workshop in Ballarat" and "Shop the pieces we ship" is a clear pair. A single button that says "Explore" makes both people guess.

Put the path that matches your actual mix first, and make the other one obvious. If most revenue is the room, the visit can be the primary action and the shop can be the second. If most revenue is the parcel, reverse it. The mistake is a hero that is only a photograph of the room, with the shop buried, while half the orders come from people who will never see the room. The matching mistake is a storefront template with no address, so the neighbor who wanted to visit cannot tell if you are real.

Say the city and the shipping fact in the same breath. "Open Thursday to Sunday in town. We ship across the country." A reader should not have to open the footer to learn which of those is true.

Hanabi's public project Down the Cove is an ecommerce migration and redesign. It is the shipment job taken seriously: the shop has to make sense as a shop. A local business adds the visit job beside it. The design work is keeping those jobs from sharing one muddy call to action.

Ballarat Box Sports is a useful contrast. A community sports brand often needs the local fact, the club, the place, and also a way to buy or register. The first screen can hold both if each has a verb. "Find a session" and "Shop the kit" can sit together. "Welcome to the family" cannot carry either.

## The visit path

The visit path answers a person who might leave the house. Where you are. When you are open. What they can do there that they cannot do online. How to arrive. What it costs, if the visit itself has a price.

Put hours where they can be seen without a treasure hunt, and put them in text, not only inside a photograph of a door. A picture of the street is a pleasure. The address as text is the thing a person copies into a map. Give them both.

Write what the visit is for. A fitting. A tasting. A class. A pickup that is faster than shipping. A showroom where the online catalog is only a fraction of the stock. If the visit is "come browse," say whether the browsed items can be taken home today. Nothing produces a worse review than a beautiful room that is actually a pickup counter, or a pickup counter the website described as an experience.

A map helps when the entrance is easy to miss. Link to the map you actually want them to use. If parking or a buzzer matters, say so in a sentence under the address. Skip the embedded map that pushes the hours below the fold on a phone. The hours are the decision. The map is the follow-through.

If you take bookings, the booking path is part of the visit, not a third business. One button: book a time. Show the length of the visit and what to bring. A form that asks for a novel before it offers a time will lose the person who was ready.

## The shipment path

The shipment path answers a person who will never see the room. What the product is. What it costs. How it arrives. How to send it back.

Lead with the product and the price. A long essay about the neighborhood can live on the visit page. On the product page it delays the facts. You can still sound like the shop. The first screen of a product should carry the name, the price, the variants that matter, and delivery.

Baymard Institute's average of documented cart-abandonment studies is 70.22 percent. A large share of abandonment is ordinary browsing. Among the reasons shoppers give, extra costs such as shipping and tax, delivery that feels too slow, a forced account, and a long checkout are ones a small shop can design for. Show the shipping cost, or the rule that determines it, before the last step. Say the delivery window in plain language. Let a person check out as a guest. Keep the form to the fields you will actually use.

Do not make the local address the only trust signal on the product page. A shopper in another city needs the return rule, the material, and a photograph of the object. The street address supports trust. It should not replace the product.

Down the Cove's lesson applies here in miniature. After a migration, the catalog, the cart, and the content have to agree. A local shop that adds online sales has the same risk: the thing on the shelf and the thing in the cart described in two voices, with two prices. One product record. One price. The visit page and the product page both read from it.

Photography should show the object at the size a buyer needs. A mood crop of the shop interior can open the visit page. It is a poor main image for a product someone has to judge through a screen. Use the interior as the second image if it explains scale or material.

## Where the two paths meet

They meet in the brand, not in a single button. Same name, same type, same tone. Hanabi would hold that in a small system: type and color in Figma, pages in Next.js, React, and TypeScript, Tailwind for the layout, Motion only where it helps and with reduced motion respected.

Write a sentence that is true for both. "Made in the workshop, sold here and shipped." Then let the paths diverge. The visit page can talk about the street. The product page can talk about the crate, the fabric, or the sizing. Shared navigation should include both verbs, visit and shop, so a person who landed on the wrong one can switch without using the back button.

Pickup is the bridge. If local customers can buy online and collect, say the rule once, in both paths. Where to collect. How soon. Whether someone will be there. Pickup is not a third brand called "click and collect experience." It is a sentence and a status.

Email and the phone number can live in the footer and on the visit page. The address in those lines should be the shop's own address, in text, and someone should actually read it. A contact path that lands in an unattended inbox is a closed door with nicer type.

The about page can tell the longer story of the place. Keep it off the product template. People buying a repeat order do not need the origin each time. People deciding whether to visit might. Link them.

## Pages you actually need

A small set covers most local shops that also ship.

A homepage with both verbs. A visit page with hours, address, and what happens in the room. A shop index grouped the way a person chooses, by use or by type, not only by what arrived this week. Product pages with price, options, shipping, and returns. A contact or booking path. A short policies page you are willing to honor.

Add a resources or care section only when the products need it. Care, sizing, and ingredients are jobs. File them by job. A journal of neighborhood photographs is optional. It should not sit between the buyer and the price.

Skip a separate "online store" brand, subdomain, and palette unless a platform constraint forces a subdomain. If it does, keep the header, the type, and the product names identical. A shopper who thinks they have left your shop will not forgive a surprise fee.

Check the phone. The visit path is often used on the street. Tap targets for call, map, and hours have to work with a thumb. The WCAG overview describes the standard as four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A hours image with no text fails the first. A map widget that traps focus fails the second. You do not need a certification speech on the page. You need the hours in text and a path a person can finish.

## What to stop competing

Stop putting the full address in the hero at the same size as the product name if shipping is the business. Stop putting a product grid in the hero if the business is the room and the grid is three items. The secondary job gets a path. It does not get to erase the primary one.

Stop using one photograph as the answer to both jobs. The room and the object can both be beautiful. They answer different questions. Art-direct them separately. Illustrator and a simple crop are enough. You do not need a new identity for the shop channel.

Stop hiding shipping behind a chat widget. The people who will abandon are often the ones who could not see the total. Baymard's list is a reminder, not a quota. Show the number, or show the rule, early enough to be kind.

If the homepage is also trying to greet a wholesale buyer, a retail visitor, and a gift shopper at once, you have a third problem. The next piece, [a homepage for a product with three audiences](/blog/a-homepage-for-a-product-with-three-audiences), is how to pick the audience that pays and give the others a path.

When you want to see how a shop and a brand can share one site without fighting, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). Bring your own constraint back to the two verbs: visit, and ship.
